title: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
claim: Our evaluation harness intercepts agent tool calls and injects benign environment errors, so unsafe responses to failures can be measured systematically.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right, dashed divider, red loop arrow back to injection layer
description: A left-to-right diagram in three labeled columns: Task requests, Error injection layer, and Error scenarios. On the left, a question-mark speech bubble sits above a stack of blue arrows that stand for task requests. In the center, a gray agent harness box holds a model panel with xAI, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI logos. Beside it are two tool modules labeled computer use and web use. caption: Our experimental enviroment for inducing and measuring agent meltdowns.
abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks. We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.
